lessons.title: Irrigation Requirements and Scheduling
lessons.body: Bananas need about 25 mm of water per week, but in hot African climates they may need up to 50 mm. A mature plant uses 20-40 liters per day. Without enough water, bunches are small and fingers don't fill. You can check soil moisture by squeezing a handful of soil from 15 cm deep. If it crumbles, it's too dry. If it drips, it's too wet. Irrigate when the top 15 cm feels dry. In dry seasons, you may need to water every 3-4 days. Early morning or late afternoon is best to reduce evaporation. A simple drip system using 2-4 liters per hour emitters, one per plant, works well. If you use furrows, let water run for 2-3 hours per week. Mulching with dry grass or banana leaves reduces water loss by half. In Uganda, farmers who irrigated during the dry season got 30% more yield. Always water deeply, not lightly, to encourage deep roots. Avoid watering the leaves to prevent fungal diseases. If you have a borehole or stream, use a pump and pipes. If not, use a watering can or bucket. For 100 plants, you need about 2,000-4,000 liters per week. That's 200-400 jerrycans. So irrigation is a serious job. Schedule irrigation based on rainfall, soil type, and plant age. Sandy soils need more frequent watering than clay. Young plants need less water but more often. Keep a simple rain gauge or use a tin can to measure rainfall. If you get 25 mm of rain in a week, you can skip irrigation. But if it's less, top up. Overwatering causes root rot and yellow leaves. So don't just pour water; check the soil first. A good rule: water when the soil is dry 2 cm below the surface. In the dry season, this may be every day. In the wet season, you may not need to irrigate at all. Always have a plan and stick to it.

lessons.title: Drip and Furrow Irrigation Methods
lessons.body: Drip irrigation saves water and is easy to manage. You need a tank, a filter, and black plastic pipes with emitters. For 100 banana plants, use a 1,000-liter tank placed 1 meter high. Connect a 16 mm drip line along each row, with one emitter per plant. Each emitter gives 2-4 liters per hour. Run the system for 1-2 hours every 2-3 days. This uses 200-400 liters per session. Drip keeps leaves dry, reducing diseases. It also allows you to apply fertilizer through the water (fertigation). In Kenya, smallholder farmers using drip on bananas saved 50% water and increased yields by 25%. You can buy drip kits from agro-dealers for about $50 for 100 plants. Clean the filter weekly and flush the lines monthly to prevent clogging. Furrow irrigation is cheaper but uses more water. Dig furrows 20 cm deep between rows. Let water flow from a canal or pipe. Water for 2-3 hours per week. This wets the root zone. But furrows can erode soil and spread weeds. In sandy soil, water disappears fast, so you may need to run furrows more often. In clay soil, water stays longer, so less frequent. Always check that water reaches the end of the furrow. If not, level the land or shorten the furrow. Furrow irrigation is best for flat land with plenty of water. Drip is best for dry areas or where water is scarce. You can combine both: drip in dry season, furrow in wet season. For either method, avoid wetting the trunk to prevent rot. Mulch between rows to reduce evaporation. With drip, you can also inject soluble fertilizers like urea or potassium. But flush the lines after fertigation. If you use furrow, apply fertilizer before watering so it dissolves and reaches roots. Always monitor soil moisture. If leaves start wilting in the afternoon, you need more water. If they stay wilted in the morning, you have overwatered or have root disease. Adjust your schedule. Remember, bananas are heavy drinkers but don't like soggy feet. Good drainage is key. If water stands for more than a day, dig drainage channels. With the right method, you can grow bananas even in dry areas.

lessons.title: Macronutrients: Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium
lessons.body: Bananas need three main nutrients: nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). Nitrogen makes leaves green and promotes growth. A mature banana plant needs about 200-300 grams of N per year. You can get this from urea (46% N) or ammonium sulphate (21% N). Apply 200 grams of urea per plant per year, split into 4 applications. Without enough N, leaves turn pale green and growth slows. Phosphorus helps roots and flowers. Bananas need about 50-100 grams of P per year. Use triple superphosphate (46% P) or rock phosphate. Apply 100 grams per plant per year at planting. P deficiency causes purple leaves and poor root development. Potassium is the most important for fruit. Bananas need 300-500 grams of K per year. Use muriate of potash (60% K) or potassium sulphate. Apply 500 grams per plant per year, split into 4 applications. K deficiency causes yellow edges on older leaves and small bunches. In Africa, many soils are depleted, so fertilizers are essential. But don't guess. Test your soil first. If you can't test, use a general recommendation: 200g N, 100g P, 500g K per plant per year. For 100 plants, that's 20 kg urea, 10 kg TSP, and 50 kg muriate of potash. Mix and apply in a ring 30 cm from the trunk. Cover with soil and water. Organic sources like manure and compost also provide these nutrients. Cattle manure has about 0.5% N, 0.2% P, and 0.5% K. So 10 kg of manure gives 50g N, 20g P, 50g K. Combine organic and mineral fertilizers for best results. Apply N and K in 4 splits: at planting, 3 months, 6 months, and 9 months. P is applied once at planting. Avoid applying fertilizer in dry soil; water first. Too much N causes lots of leaves but few bananas. Too much K can block magnesium uptake. So balance is key. Follow the 4R rule: right source, right rate, right time, right place.

lessons.title: Micronutrients and Deficiency Symptoms
lessons.body: Bananas also need small amounts of micronutrients: zinc (Zn), boron (B), iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), copper (Cu), and molybdenum (Mo). These are needed in tiny quantities but are critical. Zinc deficiency causes narrow, pointed leaves and stunted growth. You can spray zinc sulphate (0.5%) on leaves. Boron deficiency causes brittle leaves and poor fruit fill. Spray borax (0.2%) or apply 10 grams per plant. Iron deficiency causes yellow leaves with green veins, common in alkaline soils. Spray iron chelate (0.5%). Manganese deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis on young leaves. Spray manganese sulphate (0.5%). Copper deficiency causes twisted leaves. Spray copper oxychloride (0.2%). In Africa, micronutrient deficiencies are common in sandy and highly weathered soils. The best way to know is leaf tissue testing. If you can't test, look for symptoms. But be careful: too much micronutrient can be toxic. For example, boron toxicity causes leaf tip burn. So only apply if you see symptoms. A simple foliar spray with a mix of micronutrients can help. You can buy commercial mixes like 'Banana Special' or 'Micronutrient Mix'. Apply every 2-3 months. For 100 plants, mix 100 grams of each micronutrient in 100 liters of water and spray. Use a knapsack sprayer. Spray in the early morning or late evening. Add a sticker to help it stick to leaves. Organic matter helps release micronutrients. So add compost or manure. Also, keep soil pH between 6.0 and 7.0. If too acidic (below 5.5), apply lime. If too alkaline (above 7.5), apply gypsum or elemental sulphur. In Kenya, farmers who applied zinc and boron saw 20% more marketable bunches. So don't ignore micronutrients. They are the vitamins for your bananas. A balanced approach: soil test, leaf test, and visual symptoms. Then apply the right micronutrient at the right rate. Don't overdo it. A little goes a long way.

lessons.title: Fertilizer Application Techniques and Timing
lessons.body: How you apply fertilizer is as important as what you apply. For bananas, apply fertilizer in a ring around the plant, 30-50 cm from the trunk. This is where the feeder roots are. Don't put fertilizer directly against the trunk; it can burn the plant. Dig a shallow trench 5-10 cm deep, spread the fertilizer, then cover with soil. Water immediately after applying. If you use drip irrigation, you can inject soluble fertilizers into the system. This is called fertigation. Use urea, potassium nitrate, or a complete soluble fertilizer. Inject every 2 weeks during the growing season. For furrow irrigation, apply fertilizer before watering so it dissolves and moves to roots. Timing: bananas need nutrients most during active growth and bunch development. Split nitrogen and potassium into 4 applications per year: at the start of rains, mid-rainy season, end of rains, and during dry season if you irrigate. Phosphorus is applied once at planting. For a mature plant, apply 50g N, 25g P, and 125g K per application. That's 100g urea, 50g TSP, and 200g muriate of potash per plant per application. For 100 plants, that's 10 kg urea, 5 kg TSP, and 20 kg muriate of potash per application. Adjust based on soil test. Organic fertilizers like manure and compost are best applied at planting or at the start of rains. Apply 10-20 kg per plant per year, spread around the plant. Don't apply fresh manure; it can burn roots. Compost should be well-rotted. In Uganda, farmers who applied fertilizer in a ring and watered got 40% higher yields than those who broadcast. So method matters. Also, don't apply fertilizer on wet leaves; it can cause burns. Apply to soil. If you use foliar sprays, apply in the early morning or late evening. Use a surfactant. Keep records: date, amount, and type of fertilizer. This helps you learn what works. Remember, over-fertilizing wastes money and can pollute water. Under-fertilizing gives poor yields. So follow recommendations and adjust based on plant performance.

lessons.title: Soil and Leaf Tissue Testing for Nutrient Management
lessons.body: Testing your soil and leaves is the smartest way to manage nutrients. A soil test tells you what nutrients are already in the soil and what is missing. It also tells you soil pH, which affects nutrient availability. Take soil samples from 15-20 spots in your banana field. Use a clean hoe or auger. Dig 15 cm deep. Mix all samples in a clean bucket. Take about 500 grams of the mixed soil and send it to a lab. In many African countries, soil testing costs $10-30 per sample. You can find labs at agricultural research stations or universities. For leaf testing, take the third fully open leaf from the top of the plant. Sample 10-20 plants. Cut a strip of leaf blade without the midrib. Send to a lab. Leaf testing shows what the plant has actually taken up. This is more accurate than soil testing because it reflects plant health. For bananas, critical levels for leaf N are 2.5-3.0%, P 0.2-0.3%, K 2.5-3.5%. If below, you need to fertilize. If above, reduce. In Kenya, farmers who used leaf testing saved 30% on fertilizer by applying only what was needed. If you can't afford lab tests, use a simple soil test kit. These kits give rough estimates of pH, N, P, K. They cost $20-50 and can be used many times. Also, observe your plants: yellow leaves mean N deficiency, purple leaves mean P deficiency, yellow leaf edges mean K deficiency. But symptoms can be confused with diseases. So testing is best. Test every 1-2 years. Keep records of test results and fertilizer applications. This helps you track changes. For organic farmers, test manure and compost too. They vary in nutrient content. A good practice: test soil before planting, then leaf test every 6 months. Adjust fertilizer based on results. This saves money and protects the environment. Remember, healthy soil grows healthy bananas. Testing is an investment, not a cost.

quiz.q: How much water does a mature banana plant use per day?
quiz.explanation: A mature banana plant typically uses 20-40 liters of water per day.

quiz.q: What is the best time to irrigate bananas?
options: B) Early morning or late afternoon
quiz.explanation: Early morning or late afternoon reduces water loss through evaporation.

quiz.q: How can you check if soil is dry enough to irrigate?
options: B) Squeeze a handful of soil from 15 cm deep
quiz.explanation: Squeezing soil from 15 cm deep is a simple field test for moisture.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of mulching in banana farming?
options: B) Reduces water loss by half
quiz.explanation: Mulching reduces evaporation and conserves soil moisture.

quiz.q: How much water does a drip irrigation system with one 2-4 L/h emitter per plant use for 100 plants in 2 hours?
quiz.explanation: 100 plants Ã 2-4 L/h Ã 2 hours = 400-800 liters.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of furrow irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Furrow irrigation uses more water than drip and can cause erosion.

quiz.q: What is fertigation?
options: A) Applying fertilizer with irrigation water
quiz.explanation: Fertigation is the injection of soluble fertilizers into an irrigation system.

quiz.q: How often should you clean a drip irrigation filter?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning prevents clogging of emitters.

quiz.q: Which macronutrient is most important for banana fruit development?
quiz.explanation: Potassium is critical for fruit size and quality.

quiz.q: What is the recommended annual amount of nitrogen per mature banana plant?
quiz.explanation: A mature banana plant needs about 200-300 grams of nitrogen per year.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is a good source of phosphorus?
quiz.explanation: Triple superphosphate is high in phosphorus (46% P).

quiz.q: What symptom indicates potassium deficiency in bananas?
options: B) Yellow edges on older leaves
quiz.explanation: Potassium deficiency causes yellowing along the edges of older leaves.

quiz.q: How should you apply fertilizer to a banana plant?
options: B) In a ring 30-50 cm from the trunk
quiz.explanation: Applying in a ring around the plant ensures roots can access nutrients without burning the trunk.

quiz.q: Which micronutrient deficiency causes narrow, pointed leaves?
quiz.explanation: Zinc deficiency leads to narrow, pointed leaves and stunted growth.

quiz.q: What is a common symptom of iron deficiency in bananas?
options: A) Yellow leaves with green veins
quiz.explanation: Iron deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis, where leaves are yellow with green veins.

quiz.q: How can you correct boron deficiency?
quiz.explanation: A foliar spray of 0.2% borax can correct boron deficiency.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH range for banana cultivation?
quiz.explanation: Bananas grow best in soil pH between 6.0 and 7.0.

quiz.q: What is the 4R rule for fertilizer application?
options: A) Right source, right rate, right time, right place
quiz.explanation: The 4R rule ensures efficient and effective fertilizer use.

quiz.q: How often should you split nitrogen and potassium applications per year?
quiz.explanation: Splitting into 4 applications improves nutrient uptake and reduces losses.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of fertigation?
quiz.explanation: Fertigation delivers nutrients directly to roots, saving water and fertilizer.

quiz.q: How deep should you take soil samples for testing?
quiz.explanation: Soil samples for nutrient testing are typically taken from 15 cm depth.

quiz.q: Which leaf is sampled for banana leaf tissue testing?
options: B) Third fully open leaf from top
quiz.explanation: The third fully open leaf is the standard for tissue testing in bananas.

quiz.q: What is the critical leaf nitrogen level for bananas?
quiz.explanation: Leaf nitrogen should be between 2.5% and 3.0% for healthy bananas.

quiz.q: How much does soil testing typically cost in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Soil testing in Africa usually costs between $10 and $30 per sample.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for estimating soil pH and nutrients?
quiz.explanation: Soil test kits provide rough estimates of pH and nutrient levels at low cost.

quiz.q: Why is leaf testing more accurate than soil testing?
options: A) It shows what the plant has taken up
quiz.explanation: Leaf testing reflects the actual nutrient status of the plant.

quiz.q: What should you do if leaf test shows potassium above critical level?
quiz.explanation: If potassium is above critical level, reduce or skip potassium application to avoid waste and imbalance.

quiz.q: How often should you test soil and leaves?
options: B) Every 1-2 years for soil, every 6 months for leaves
quiz.explanation: Soil testing every 1-2 years and leaf testing every 6 months is recommended.

quiz.q: What is a risk of over-fertilizing with nitrogen?
options: A) Lots of leaves but few bananas
quiz.explanation: Excess nitrogen promotes vegetative growth at the expense of fruit production.

quiz.q: Which organic material is a good source of potassium?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is rich in potassium and can be used as a supplement.
